sections.title: The person who feels is the subject
sections.content: In Lesson 1 the feeling was the subject and the person was the indirect object (*me molesta*). With *sentir*, *lamentar* and *temer* it is the other way round: the person who feels is the subject, so the verb changes with the person (*siento*, *lamentamos*, *temen*). You know *sentir* from A2 Unit 27 and *lamentar* from B2 Unit 4. The clause after *que* is still in the subjunctive when it has a different subject.

sections.title: Three verbs of feeling
rows: I'm sorry that... / I regret that...
Same person on both verbs: Lamento llegar tarde (I am the one arriving late).

sections.title: Same person or a different one?
sections.content: You know *Quiero comer* and *Quiero que comas* from B2 Unit 4: the same rule applies here. *Lamento llegar tarde* (I am late) but *Lamento que llegues tarde* (you are late).

sections.title: Careful with sentir que
sections.content: *Sentir que* has two meanings. When you are sorry, it takes the subjunctive: *Siento que estés enfermo* (I'm sorry you are ill). When it means 'I feel that' or 'I have the impression that', it takes the indicative: *Siento que algo no está bien*.

items.spanish: Siento que tengas que trabajar este fin de semana.
items.english: I'm sorry that you have to work this weekend.

items.spanish: Lamentamos que no hayan podido venir.
items.english: We are sorry that they have not been able to come.

items.spanish: Temo que la reunión termine muy tarde.
items.english: I'm afraid that the meeting will finish very late.

items.spanish: Temíamos que el tren llegara tarde.
items.english: We were afraid that the train would arrive late.

sections.content: To offer condolences after a death, say *Mi más sentido pésame* or *Les doy el pésame*. For something smaller, *Lo siento mucho* is enough.
